L560: ## \sectionrule 3ex0pt-1ex1pt5 \sectionrule 3ex0pt-1ex1ptWeighted colimits and semi-tropical modules
L561: 
L562: In this section we see the definition and some examples of the notion of weighted colimit in the context of generalized metric spaces. We then see how the idea of having all colimits is related to being a module over the semi-tropical semiring. There is a completely dual story involving the notion of weighted limit. We will need the dual story but will summarize those results later.
L563: ### 5.1 Definition
L564: 
L565: We will look at the definition of weighted colimit and associated concepts and at some examples.
L566: 
L567: The concept of weighted (or indexed) colimit is natural in the context of enriched categories and generalizes the concept of ordinary colimit in ordinary category theory. We will usually just refer to colimits, dropping the prefix weighted.
L568: In order to define a weighted colimit in a generalized metric space $X$ we need some ingredients. A shape $D$ is a generalized metric space; a diagram of shape $D$ is a short map $J\colon D\to X$; and a weighting is a presheaf $W\colon D^{{\mathrm{op}}}\to[0,\infty]$. A colimit of the diagram $J$ with weighting $W$ is an object $c$ of $X$ which satisfies
L569: 
L570:  | $$\dd_{X}(c,x)=\sup_{d\in D}\bigl\{\dd_{X}(J(d),x)\mminus W(d)\bigr\}\qquad\text{for all }x\in X.$$  |
L571: This is not a terribly enlightening definition but hopefully the meaning will become clearer after some examples below, we perhaps want to think of it as a weighted sum,
L572: 
L573:  | $$\text{``}c=\sum_{d\in D}W(d)\cdot J(d)\text{''},$$  |
L574: 
L575: or, to use symbols more commonly used in tropical mathematics,
L576: 
L577:  | $$\text{``}c=\bigoplus_{d\in D}W(d)\odot J(d)\text{''}.$$  |
L578: This idea will be made precise later. There is a slight notation clash here in that $\oplus$ is often used in category theory for things which are both products and coproducts, but we won’t mean that sense here.
L579: For a given $W$ and $J$ a colimit might or might not exist, and if it does exist then in general there might be other isomorphic colimits. However, if $X$ is skeletal then colimits, when they exist, are uniquely defined. We write $\operatorname{colim}_{W}(J)$ for ‘the’ colimit of $W$ and $J$ if it exists, so if $c$ is a colimit we can write $c\simeq\operatorname{colim}_{W}(J)$.
L580: A generalized metric space which has colimits for all diagrams and weightings is said to be cocomplete. If it has colimits for all diagrams and weightings on shapes which are finite then it is said to be finitely cocomplete.
L581: A short map $F\colon X\to Y$ is called cocontinuous if it preserves colimits in the sense that for any $J\colon D\to X$ and $W\colon D^{\mathrm{op}}\to[0,\infty]$ for which the colimit $\operatorname{colim}_{W}(J)$ exists we have $F(\operatorname{colim}_{W}(J))\simeq\operatorname{colim}_{W}(F\circ J)$. It is worth recording here for later use that left adjonts are cocontinuous.
L582: ###### Lemma 8.
L583: 
L584: If $F\colon X\to Y$ is a short map is short map between generalized metric space with a right adjoint then $F$ is cocontinuous.
L585: ###### Proof.
L586: 
L587: Let $G\colon Y\to X$ be the right adjoint. Suppose that $J\colon D\to X$ is a diagram and $W\colon D^{\mathrm{op}}\to[0,\infty]$ is a weighting such that the colimit $\operatorname{colim}_{W}(J)$ exists. Then we use the adjointness twice to see
L588:  | $\displaystyle\dd_{Y}(F(\operatorname{colim}_{W}(J)),y)$  | $\displaystyle=\dd_{X}(\operatorname{colim}_{W}(J),G(y))$  |
L589:  |  | $\displaystyle=\dd_{\widehat{D}}\Bigl(W({-}),\dd_{X}\bigl(J({-}),G(y)\bigr)\Bigr)$  |
L590:  |  | $\displaystyle=\dd_{\widehat{D}}\Bigl(W({-}),\dd_{X}(F\circ J({-}),y)\Bigr),$  |
L591: 
L592: thus $F(\operatorname{colim}_{W}(J))\simeq\operatorname{colim}_{W}(F\circ J)$. So $F$ is cocontinuous as required. ∎
L593: Note that the definition of the colimit does not say anything about the distance to the colimit; we will come back to this later in Section cite31†6.2 .
L594: ### 5.2 Examples
L595: 
L596: We can now have a look at some examples.
L597: #### 5.2.1 Initial points
L598: 
L599: If the shape $D$ is the empty metric space $\emptyset$ then we use the unique maps $\emptyset\to X$ and $\emptyset\to[0,\infty]$, and as the supremum of an empty subset of $[0,\infty]$ is $0$ we get that a colimit, denoted by $\top$ satisfies
L600: 
L601:  | $$\dd(\top,x)=0\qquad\text{for all }x\in X.$$  |
L602: So a colimit $\top$ of the empty diagram is to be thought of as some sort of ‘initial’ point, being a distance $0$ to every other point. Classical metric spaces with more than one point can not have an initial point, but as we have seen, the Isbell completion of a metric space can have an initial point. The asymmetric extended non-negative reals $[0,\infty]$ has $\infty$ as an initial point.
L603: #### 5.2.2 Fat out points
L604: 
L605: If the shape $D$ is a singleton metric space $\{\ast\}$ with the diagram $J$ mapping to the point $x_{0}\in X$ and the weighting $W$ taking the value $r\in[0,\infty]$, then the colimit $O(x_{0},r)$ satisfies
L606: 
L607:  | $$\dd_{X}(O(x_{0},r),x)=\dd_{X}(x_{0},x)\mminus r,$$  |
L608: 
L609: so can be thought of as a “fat out point” at $x_{0}$ of radius $r$. See Figure cite82†6 . I’d rather think of this as a fat point than a ball, as a ball has many points in it.
L610: 
L611: Figure 6: A fat out point.
L612: A classical metric space will typically not have such colimits. The asymmetric metric space $[0,\infty]$ does have such fat out points: in that case $O(x_{0},r)=x_{0}+r$.
L613: #### 5.2.3 Coproducts
L614: 
L615: If the shape $D$ consists of two points infinitely far apart, and we take the weighting $W$ to be the zero weighting, then writing $x_{1},x_{2}\in X$ for the images of the two points under $J$ and $x_{1}\sqcup x_{2}$ for the colimit, we have
L616: 
L617:  | $$\dd(x_{1}\sqcup x_{2},x)=\max\bigl(\dd(x_{1},x),\dd(x_{2},x)\bigr)\qquad\text{for all }x\in X.$$  |
L618: So $x_{1}\sqcup x_{2}$ should be thought of as a coproduct. Again, in general, classical metric spaces will not have coproducts, however $[0,\infty]$ does, with $x_{1}\sqcup x_{2}=\min(x_{1},x_{2})$.
L619: #### 5.2.4 Limits of sequences
L620: 
L621: If the shape $D$ is the set of natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ with infinite distance between each pair of points, then a diagram $\mathbb{N}\to X$ is the same thing as a sequence in $X$. Rutten [cite47†17 , Propostion 1.1] showed how Cauchy sequences can be examined using weighted limits and colimits.
L622: #### 5.2.5 The asymmetric space $[0,\infty]$ is cocomplete
L623: 
L624: The generalized metric space $[0,\infty]$ with its standard asymmetric metric has all colimits. Given a diagram $J\colon D\to[0,\infty]$ and a weighting $W\colon D^{{\mathrm{op}}}\to[0,\infty]$ the colimit is given by
L625: 
L626:  | $$\operatorname{colim}_{J}(F)=\inf_{d\in D}(W(d)+J(d)).$$  |
L627: I will leave the reader to draw the appropriate pictures of fat points, and deduce that this is immediately clear. On the other hand, the symmetric metric structure of $[0,\infty]$ does not have such arbitrary colimits.
L628: ### 5.3 Characterizing cocompleteness
L629: If we wish to show that a generalized metric space has all colimits then it suffices to consider shapes in which all of the the distances are infinite, we call these discrete shapes. If $D$ is a generalized metric space, then there is a discrete metric space $D^{\delta}$ called the discretization of $D$ which has the same points as $D$, but has all non-zero distances becoming infinite.
L630: There is an identity-on-points short map $\delta\colon D^{\delta}\to D$ and we can pull back any $D$-shaped diagram to a $D^{\delta}$-shaped diagram. Now using this we see that every colimit can be written as a colimit of a discrete diagram.
L631: ###### Theorem 9.
L632: 
L633: If $J\colon D\to X$ is a diagram then by pulling back we get a diagram $\delta^{*}J\colon D^{\delta}\to X$ and a discrete weighting $\delta^{*}W\colon D^{\delta}\to[0,\infty]$. If $\operatorname{colim}_{\delta^{*}W}(\delta^{*}J)$ exists then
L634: 
L635:  | $$\operatorname{colim}_{\delta^{*}W}(\delta^{*}J)\simeq\operatorname{colim}_{W}(J).$$  |
L636: ###### Proof.
L637: 
L638: If the colimit exists then we have
L639:  | $\displaystyle\dd_{X}(\operatorname{colim}_{\delta^{*}W}(\delta^{*}J),x)$  | $\displaystyle=\dd_{\widehat{D^{\delta}}}\Bigl(\delta^{*}W\left({-}\right),\dd_{X}\bigl(\delta^{*}J\left({-}\right),x\bigr)\Bigr)$  |
L640:  |  | $\displaystyle=\sup_{d\in D^{\delta}}\left\{\dd_{[0,\infty]}\Bigl(W\circ\delta(d),\dd_{X}\bigl(J\circ\delta(d),x\bigr)\Bigr)\right\}$  |
L641:  |  | $\displaystyle=\sup_{d\in D}\biggl\{\dd_{[0,\infty]}\Bigl(W({d}),\dd_{X}\bigl(J({d}),x\bigr)\Bigr)\biggr\}$  |
L642:  |  | $\displaystyle=\dd_{\widehat{D}}\Bigl(W({-}),\dd_{X}\bigl(J({-}),x\bigr)\Bigr).$  |
L643: Thus $\operatorname{colim}_{\delta^{*}W}(\delta^{*}J)\simeq\operatorname{colim}_{W}(J)$ as required. ∎
L644: 
L645: We immediately get the following corollary.
L646: ###### Corollary 10.
L647: 
L648: If $X$ has colimits for all weightings on discrete shapes then $X$ has all colimits, i.e. $X$ is cocomplete.
L649: 
L650: Similarly, If $X$ has colimits for all weightings on finite discrete shapes then $X$ has all finite colimits, i.e. $X$ is finitely cocomplete.
L651: 
L652: We can now characterize cocomplete generalized metric spaces as follows.
L653: 
L654: ###### Lemma 11.
L655: 
L656: If a generalized metric space $X$ has an binary products and all fat out points then it has all finite colimits.
L657: ###### Proof.
L658: By the above it suffices to prove that any discrete diagram $J$ and weighting $W$ has a colimit. We proceed by induction on the number of objects in the shape $D$. If $D=\emptyset$ then the colimit is the initial point which is given by the fat out point $O(x,\infty)$ for any $x\in X$. If $D$ is not empty then we can write $D=D^{\prime}\cup\{d\}$ and it is straightforward to show that $\operatorname{colim}_{W}(J)=\operatorname{colim}_{{W|_{D^{\prime}}}}(J|_{D^{\prime}})\sqcup O(J(d),W(d))$.

L52: # Tight spans, Isbell completions and semi-tropical modules.
L53: 
L54: Simon Willerton
L55: ###### Abstract
L56: In this paper we consider generalized metric spaces in the sense of Lawvere and the categorical Isbell completion construction. We show that this is an analogue of the tight span construction of classical metric spaces, and that the Isbell completion coincides with the directed tight span of Hirai and Koichi.
L57: The notions of categorical completion and cocompletion are related to the existence of semi-tropical module structure, and it is shown that the Isbell completion (hence the directed tight span) has two different semi-tropical module structures.

L69: This paper grew out of a desire to understand whether the tight span of a metric space could be understood in terms of the enriched category theory approach to metric spaces. This led to understanding a link between two apparently unrelated constructions of Isbell, namely the tight span of metric spaces and the Isbell completion of categories; this is turn led, via categorical completeness, to connections with tropical algebra.
L70: In this introduction the main ideas of Isbell completion, semi-tropical algebra and tight spans will be given. The intention is that this paper should be readable by mathematicians interested in metric spaces or tropical algebra, without much category theory background, and to allow them to see how category theoretic methods give interesting insight in this case.
L71: ### The Isbell completion of a generalized metric space
L72: Lawvere [cite40†13 ] observed that a metric space can be viewed as something similar to a category and that from that perspective there is a natural generalization — generalized metric space — which means a set $X$ with a ‘distance’ function $\dd\colon X\times X\to[0,\infty]$ such that $\dd(x,x)=0$ and $\dd(x,y)+\dd(y,z)\geq\dd(x,z)$ for all $x,y,z\in X$, with no further conditions like symmetry imposed. Generalized metric spaces can be thought of as ‘directed’ metric spaces.

L111: The other, metric, semi-tropical module structure is similarly calculated using $\iota^{2}\colon I(X)\to\widecheck{X}^{\mathrm{op}}$, and the retraction $LR\colon\widecheck{X}^{\mathrm{op}}\to I(X)$.
L112: ### The tight span
L113: Every classical metric space $\mathsf{X}$ has a ‘tight span’ $T(\mathsf{X})$. This has been discovered independently on several occasions and goes by many names. Isbell called it the injective envelope [cite56†10 ], Dress called it the tight span [cite57†6 ] and Chrobak and Larmore called it the convex hull [cite58†3 ]. Two good introductions to the theory of tight spans are [cite59†7 ] and [cite60†8 ].
L114: One naive way of thinking of the tight span is that it is a ‘small’ contractible metric space in which the metric space embeds isometrically, but the full story is somewhat richer than that. An example of the three-point metric space is pictured in Figure cite46†1 .
L115: In general the tight span of a finite metric space is a finite cell complex of dimension at most half the number of points in $\mathsf{X}$, i.e. $\dim T(\mathsf{X})\leq\frac{1}{2}\#\mathsf{X}$. A metric space embeds into a tree if and only if the tight span is a tree, because of this the tight span has become a useful tool in phylogenetic analysis [cite59†7 ]. The tight span also has applications in group cohomology [cite57†6 ], server placement on a network [cite58†3 ] and multicommodity flow [cite61†11 ].
L116: Develin and Sturmfels [cite62†4 , cite63†5 ] showed connections with tropical mathematics, showing in some cases that the tight span was related to the tropical hull of the metric.
L117: The tight span is related to the Isbell completion in the following way (Theorem cite64†6 ). For a classical metric space $\mathsf{X}$ the tight span $T(\mathsf{X})$ is the largest subset of of the Isbell completion $I(\mathsf{X})$ which contains $\mathsf{X}$ and for which the restriction of the generalized metric is actually a classical metric.
L118: Having understood the connection between Isbell’s tight span and the Isbell completion, I discovered that, motivated by applications in multicommodity flow, Hirai and Koichi [cite65†9 ] had constructed an analogue of the tight span for what they called finite ‘directed’ metric spaces, by which they meant a space with the structure of a classical metric space, except that the symmetry axiom $\dd(x,y)=\dd(y,x)$ is not imposed.
L119: For a directed metric space $X$ we will denote their ‘directed tight span’ by $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{HK}}(X)$. In Theorem cite66†7 we see that for directed metric spaces the directed tight span and the Isbell completion coincide: $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{HK}}(X)\cong I(X)$. From the semi-tropical module structures described above, we immediately get the following.
L120: ###### Theorem.
L121: 
L122: For a directed metric space, the directed tight span of Hirai and Koichi can be given two canonical semi-tropical module structures.

L127: ## \sectionrule 3ex0pt-1ex1pt1 \sectionrule 3ex0pt-1ex1ptMetric spaces as enriched categories, briefly
L128: In this section we give a give introduction to the idea of viewing metric spaces as enriched categories. This gives rise to Lawvere’s notion of generalized metric space. We give the relevant concepts from enriched category theory in this context, one of the most important concepts here being that of the generalized metric space of presheaves; a presheaf being the appropriate notion of scalar-valued function on a space. References for this include [cite40†13 , cite67†12 , cite68†2 ].
L129: We finish the section by mentioning adjunctions and state the idempotent property exhibited by metric space adjunctions.
L130: Recall that a small category $\mathcal{C}$ consists of a set $\Ob(\mathcal{C})$ of objects together with the following data, satisfying the so-called ‘associativity’ and ‘unit’ axioms.

L135:

L138: For each $c\in\Ob(\mathcal{C})$ there is an identity morphism; equivalently, there is a specified function $\{\ast\}\to\Hom_{\mathcal{C}}(c,c)$.

L204: ## \sectionrule 3ex0pt-1ex1pt2 \sectionrule 3ex0pt-1ex1ptIsbell’s tight span in category-theoretic language
L205: In this section we state Isbell’s original definition of the tight span, his ‘injective envelope’, and then reformulate it in a fashion amenable to a category theoretic analysis. We then compare the two approaches in some simple examples, seeing that the two approaches, but not the final answers, are indeed somewhat different. Throughout this section we use a sans serif symbol such as $\mathsf{X}$ to denote a classical metric space.
L206: Whilst in the literature the tight span and the injective envelope are used to mean the same thing, here I will use the terminology to distinguish two isometric metric spaces.
L207: ### 2.1 Two definitions of the tight span
L208: 
L209: Isbell, in his 1964 paper [cite56†10 ], constructs for a classical metric space $\mathsf{X}$ the ‘injective envelope’ $\mathcal{E}(\mathsf{X})$ in the following way. Firstly define $\Aim(\mathsf{X})$ the aim of $\mathsf{X}$ by $f\in\Aim(\mathsf{X})$ if $f$ is a real-valued function on $\mathsf{X}$ which satisfies
L210: 
L211:  | $$f(x)+f(y)\geq\dd(x,y)\quad\text{for all }x,y\in\mathsf{X}.$$  |
L212: A function $f\in\Aim(\mathsf{X})$ is pointwise-minimal if whenever $g\in\Aim(\mathsf{X})$ satisfies $g(x)\leq f(x)$ for all $x\in\mathsf{X}$ then $g=f$. We then define the injective envelope $\mathcal{E}(\mathsf{X})$ to be the classical metric space of pointwise-minimal functions in $\Aim(\mathsf{X})$, with the metric on $\mathcal{E}(\mathsf{X})$ given by
L213: 
L214:  | $$\dd_{\mathcal{E}(\mathsf{X})}(f,g)=\sup_{x\in\mathsf{X}}|f(x)-g(x)|.$$  |
L215: That is the standard definition of the injective envelope or tight span, however, we can characterize it in the following way which is amenable to the category theoretic approach. Let the tight span $T(\mathsf{X})\subset\widehat{\mathsf{X}}$ be the subset of presheaves on $\mathsf{X}$ such that a presheaf $f\colon\mathsf{X}\to[0,\infty]$ is in $T(\mathsf{X})$ if
L216: 
L217:  | $$f(x)=\sup_{y\in\mathfrak{\mathsf{X}}}\bigl(\dd(x,y)\mminus f(y)\bigr)\quad\text{for all }x\in\mathsf{X}.$$  |
L218: The metric on $T(\mathsf{X})$ is induced from the generalized metric on $\widehat{\mathsf{X}}$. A calculation shows that the metric on $T(\mathsf{X})$ is actually symmetric.
L219: These two definitions are equivalent in that there is a canonical isomorphism of metric spaces $\mathcal{E}(\mathsf{X})\cong T(\mathsf{X})$: indeed, in some sense, they have the same set of points; however, they are defined as subspaces of different spaces. The details of the proof that they are isometric are given by Dress [cite57†6 ]; the subtle part is showing that the metrics actually agree. Theorem cite66†7 generalizes this result and the proof given there is a generalization of Dress’ proof.
L220: Before comparing the injective envelope $\mathcal{E}(\mathsf{X})$ and the tight span $T(\mathsf{X})$ in some examples, it is worth noting two things about the tight span. The first thing is that $\mathsf{X}$ maps isometrically in to its tight-span $T(\mathsf{X})$ via the Yoneda map:
L221: 
L222:  | $$\Yoneda\colon\mathsf{X}\to T(\mathsf{X});\qquad x\mapsto\dd({-},x).$$  |
L223: The second is that one can interpret the condition (cite70†2.1 ) as follows. The idea is that a function $f$ represents a point, say $p_{f}$, in an extension of $\mathsf{X}$ with $\dd(p_{f},x)=f(x)$ for all $x\in\mathsf{X}$.
L224: The supremum condition (cite70†2.1 ) on $f$ is saying that “for every point $x\in\mathsf{X}$ the point $p_{f}$ is arbitrarily close to being on a geodesic from $x$ to another point”; in other terms, for all $\varepsilon\geq 0$ there is a $y$ such that $\dd(x,p_{f})+\dd(p_{f},y)\leq d(x,y)+\varepsilon$. This is expressing the minimality of the tight-span $T(\mathsf{X})$, saying that the points of $T(\mathsf{X})$ must ‘lie between’ the points of $\mathsf{X}$.
L225: ### 2.2 Examples
L226: 
L227: Here are two examples which compare the two approaches to the tight span.
L228: The two-point metric space $A_{r}$ is pictured in Figure cite71†3 . We define $\Aim(A_{r})\in\mathbb{R}^{\{a,b\}}$ by $f\in\Aim(A_{r})$ if $f(a)+f(b)\geq r$, $f(a)\geq 0$, and $f(b)\geq 0$. The minimal functions are those satisfying $f(a)+f(b)=r$. This defines the injective envelope $\mathcal{E}(A_{r})$ and is pictured in Figure cite71†3 . On the other hand the presheaf space $\widehat{A_{r}}\subset[0,\infty]^{\{a,b\}}$ is defined by $f\in\widehat{A_{r}}$ if $\left|f(a)-f(b)\right|\leq r$.
L229: This is also pictured in Figure cite71†3 with the tight span also drawn.
L230: The three-point classical metric space $A_{r,s,t}$ is also pictured in Figure cite71†3 . Note that the injective envelope $\mathcal{E}(A_{r,s,t})$ and the tight span $T(A_{r,s,t})$ are defined as subsets of different spaces but are isometric.

For a generalized metric space $X$, the Isbell adjunction is the following pair of maps between the spaces of presheaves and op-co-presheaves.

L495: ## \sectionrule 3ex0pt-1ex1pt4 \sectionrule 3ex0pt-1ex1ptThe Isbell completion and the tight span
L496: 
L497: In this section we show that the tight span of a classical metric space is contained in the Isbell completion. We then prove that the directed tight span of Hirai and Koichi coincides with the Isbell completion.
L498: 
L499: ### 4.1 The classical tight span
L500: 
L501: Here we show that the Isbell’s tight span of a classical metric space is contained in the Isbell completion of the metic space.
L502: ###### Theorem 6.
L503: 
L504: If $\mathsf{X}$ is a classical metric space then the tight span $T(\mathsf{X})$ is (isometric to) the maximal classical metric space inside the generalized metric space $I(\mathsf{X})$ which contains the image of $\mathsf{X}$.
L505: ###### Proof.
L506: 
L507: In Section cite8†2.1 the tight span $T(\mathsf{X})\subset\widehat{\mathsf{X}}$ is characterized by
L508: 
L509:  | $$T(\mathsf{X})=\bigl\{f\in\widehat{\mathsf{X}}\bigm|f(x)=\sup_{y\in\mathsf{X}}(\dd(x,y)\mminus f(y))\quad\text{for all }x\in\mathsf{X}\bigr\}.$$  |
L510: As $\mathsf{X}$ is symmetric, presheaves and copresheaves are the same thing, so there is a well-defined function $T(\mathsf{X})\hookrightarrow I(\mathsf{X})$ given by $f\mapsto(f,f)$. Indeed it can be seen that $T(\mathsf{X})$ is actually a subset of $\Fix_{RL}(X)\in\widehat{\mathsf{X}}$ and so inherits the same generalized metric, meaning that the inclusion is an isometry.
L511: To see that it is the maximal classical metric subspace containing $\mathsf{X}$ observe than any point $(f,g)\in I(\mathsf{X})$ inside a classical metric subspace containing $\mathsf{X}$ must have the same distance both to and from any given point of $\mathsf{X}$, in other words we must have $f=g$, thus $(f,g)\in T(\mathsf{X})$ and so $T(\mathsf{X})$ is maximal. ∎
L512: 
L513: This is illustrated in Figures cite74†4 and cite46†1 .
L514: ### 4.2 The directed tight span of Hirai and Koichi
L515: For a finite generalized metric space with no infinite distances, Hirai and Koichi [cite65†9 ] defined a ‘tight span’ which they denoted $T_{\mu}$, where $\mu$ was the generalized metric. For a generalized metric space $X$ we will use the notation $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{HK}}(X)$ and refer to it as the Hirai-Koichi tight span. Their definition is analogous to what, for a classical metric space $\mathsf{X}$, we called the injective envelope $\mathcal{E}(\mathsf{X})$.
L516: The definition can be easily generalized to all generalized metric spaces as follows.
L517: Let $P(X)$ be the set of pairs $(f,g)$ of functions $f,g\colon X\to[0,\infty]$ such that
L518: 
L519:  | $$f(x)+g(y)\geq\dd(x,y)\quad\text{for all }x,y\in X.$$  |
L520: We will call such pairs triangular, as the above inequality is supposed to be suggestive of the triangle inequality: $f(x)$ being like the distance from $x$ to the ‘point’ $(f,g)$ and $g(y)$ being like the distance from that ‘point’ to $y$. A triangular pair $(f,g)\in P(X)$ is said to be minimal if for any triangular pair $(f^{\prime},g^{\prime})\in P(X)$ such that for all $x,y\in X$ we have $f^{\prime}(x)\leq f(x)$ and $g^{\prime}(y)\leq g(y)$ then $(f^{\prime},g^{\prime})=(f,g)$.
L521: The Hirai-Koichi tight span $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{HK}}(X)$ is defined to be the set of minimal triangular pairs in $P(X)$, it is equipped with the following metric:
L522:  | $$\dd_{\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{HK}}(X)}\left((f,g),(f^{\prime},g^{\prime})\right):=\sup_{x\in X}\left\{\max\left(f^{\prime}(x)\mminus f(x),g^{\prime}(x)\mminus g(x)\right)\right\}.$$  |
L523: 
L524: We can now show that this coincides with the Isbell completion.
L525: ###### Theorem 7.
L526: 
L527: For a generalized metric space $X$, the Isbell completion and Hirai-Koichi tight span coincide, conisdered as subspaces of the same generalized metric space:
L528: 
L529:  | $$I(X)=\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{HK}}(X)\subset\left([0,\infty]^{X}\times[0,\infty]^{X}\right)_{\mathrm{asym}}.$$  |
L530: ###### Proof.
L531: 
L532: As both the Hirai-Koichi tight span and the Isbell completion are both submetric spaces of the same generalized metric spaces it suffices to prove that $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{HK}}(X)\subset I(X)$ and that $I(X)\subset\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{HK}}(X)$.
L533: To show that $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{HK}}(X)\subset I(X)$ we need to show that for any minimal triangular pair $(f,g)\in P(X)$ we have that $f$ is a presheaf, $g$ is a co-presheaf, $L(f)=g$ and $f=R(g)$. To see that $f$ is a presheaf, fix $x$ and $y$ and define a function $f_{xy}$ by
L534: 
L535:  | $$f_{xy}(w):=\begin{cases}f(y)+\dd(x,y)&\text{for }w=x\\
L536: f(w)&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$  |
L537: then the pair $(f_{xy},g)$ is triangular and so by the minimality of $(f,g)$ we must have $f_{xy}(x)\geq f(x)$. From this we obtain
L538: 
L539:  | $$\dd(x,y)\geq f(x)\mminus f(y)$$  |
L540: 
L541: and so $f$ is a presheaf. The proof that $g$ is a co-presheaf is analogous .
L542: 
L543: Now to show that $g=L(f)$, fix $y\in X$. As $(f,g)$ is triangular,
L544: 
L545:  | $$g(y)\geq\dd(x,y)\mminus f(x)\quad\text{for all }x\in X.$$  |

L128: ###### Lemma 1
L129: 
L130: A point $(x_{0},y_{0})\in\mathbb{R}^{2}_{1}$ lies between $(x_{1},y_{1})$ and $(x_{2},y_{2})\in\mathbb{R}^{2}_{1}$ in the sense of Menger if and only if $x_{0}$ lies between $x_{1}$ and $x_{2}$ (in $\mathbb{R}$) and $y_{0}$ lies between $y_{1}$ and $y_{2}$ ($x_{1}\leq x_{0}\leq x_{2}$ or $x_{2}\leq x_{0}\leq x_{1}$, respectively for $y_{0}$).
L131: Recall that $\triangle_{(x_{0},y_{0}),(x_{1},y_{1})(x_{2},y_{2})}=0$ if and only if $(x_{0},y_{0})$ lies between $(x_{1},y_{1})$ and $(x_{2},y_{2})$.
L132: 
L133: Now, we give a criterion for a finite subset of $\mathbb{R}^{2}_{1}$ to be trim:
L134: ###### Proposition 1
L135: 
L136: Let $(X,d_{1})\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}_{1}$ be a finite subspace with $|X|\geq 4$. Let $R_{X}$ denote the minimal rectangle in $\mathbb{R}^{2}_{1}$ containing $X$ with edges parallel to the axes. Then, $X$ is trim if and only if each edge of $R_{X}$ contains at least two points of $X$.
L137: Proof. First assume that $X$ is trim. Without loss of generality consider the right edge of $R_{X}$. There must be at least one point of $X$ on this edge, since otherwise the rectangle would not be minimal. Assume, there is only one point of $X$ on this edge, say $(x_{0},y_{0})$.
L138: If $(x_{1},y_{1})$ and $(x_{2},y_{2})$ are two other points of $X$, then necessarily $x_{1}<x_{0}$ and $x_{2}<x_{0}$ so that by Lemma cite23†1 , $\triangle_{(x_{0},y_{0}),(x_{1},y_{1})(x_{2},y_{2})}>0$ and then $\underline{d}_{1}((x_{0},y_{0}))>0$ since $X$ is finite. This contradicts the assumption that $X$ is trim. So, there must be at least two points of $X$ on the considered edge of $R_{X}$.
L139: Conversely, let us assume that each edge of $R_{X}$ contains at least two points of $X$. Now, a point of $X$ can be on the boundary or inside of $R_{X}$. First, consider a point $(x_{0},y_{0})\in X$ lying on an edge of $R_{X}$, say without loss of generality, on the right edge. Then choose another point $(x_{0},y_{1})\in X$ on the same edge and a third point $(x_{2},y_{2})\in X$ on the top or bottom edge of $R_{X}$ such that $y_{0}$ lies between $y_{1}$ and $y_{2}$ (see Figure cite24†4 ).
L140: Then by the Lemma cite23†1 , $\triangle_{(x_{0},y_{0}),(x_{0},y_{1})(x_{2},y_{2})}=0$ and then $\underline{d}_{1}((x_{0},y_{0}))=0$.
L141: Now, let us assume that $(x_{0},y_{0})\in X$ lies in the interior of $R_{X}$. Divide the rectangle $R_{X}$ with four subrectangles by the vertical and horizontal lines passing through $(x_{0},y_{0})$ (see Figure cite25†5 ). There must be “boundary” points of $X$ (i.e. points of $X$ lying on the boundary of $R_{X}$) either on both of the subrectangles $\rm{I}$ and $\rm{III}$, or on both of the subrectangles $\rm{II}$ and $\rm{IV}$.

L237: We then define a secondary rectangle $S_{X}=[x_{2},x_{n-1}]\times[y_{2},y_{n-1}]$ (see Figure cite28†7 ). Recall that $R_{X}$ was the minimal, axes-parallel rectangle containing $X$, which can be expressed with these notations as $R_{X}=[x_{1},x_{n}]\times[y_{1},y_{n}]$.

L240: The following proposition gives a nice device to determine the metric center $m(X):$
L241: ###### Proposition 2
L242: 
L243: The metric center $m_{a}$ of a point $a\in X$ is the point of $S_{X}$ nearest to $a$ (with respect to the $d_{1}-$metric, or what the same is, with respect to the Euclidean metric; we call this point the projection of $a$ on $S_{X}$). Especially, for a point $a\in X$ belonging to $S_{X}$, we get $m_{a}=a$. The metric center $m(X)$ of $X$ thus consists of the points of $X$ contained in $S_{X}$ and the projections of the points of $X$ outside $S_{X}$ onto $S_{X}$.

L247: We first remark that by the minimality of $R_{X}$ there exists at least one point on every edge of $R_{X}$ belonging to $X$ and all points of $X$ lying in the interior of $R_{X}$ are in-between points (i.e. have zero pendant length), so that their metric centers coincide with them.
L248: We next remark that, in cases one edge of $S_{X}$ is contained in an edge of $R_{X}$, there must be at least two points of $X$ on this edge of $R_{X}$ by the definition of $S_{X}$ and in such a case, points of $X$ lying in the corresponding edge of $S_{X}$ must be in-between points since one can use auxiliary points on approximate neighbouring edges of $R_{X}$ to see this. Thus, these points also coincide with their metric centers.
L249: Now, there remain the points of $X$, which lie on the boundary of $R_{X}$ but do not belong to $S_{X}$. L255: ## 4 How to Embed the Trimming Cylinder into the Manhattan Plane?
L256: We have seen in Theorem cite31†1 that the space $(t(X),d^{1})$, obtained by trimming a finite subspace $(X,d_{1})\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}_{1}$, can be isometrically embedded into the $\mathbb{R}^{2}_{1}$, by the canonical map $\overline{x}\mapsto m_{x}$, sending a class to the metric center of a representant of it. This enables us to work with the embedded version of the abstract trimming sequence, which we called the metric center sequence. This procedure can be extended to the trimming cylinder also.
L257: We can define the corresponding metric center cylinder $MC(X)$ as a pseudo-metric graph with the vertex set $\bigsqcup_{i\geq 0}m^{i}(X)$ and edges between $a_{i}\in m^{i}(X)$ and $g_{i}(a_{i})\in m^{i+1}(X)$ with weight $\underline{d}_{1}(a_{i})$. It is instructive to look at the first portion $MC_{1}(X)$ of this cylinder (which repeats itself in the following stages since in every stage the starting space is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{2}_{1}$):
L258: The edge between $x\in X$ and $p(x)\in t(X)$ in $C_{1}(X)$ has weight $\underline{d}_{1}(x)$; the edge between $x\in X$ and $g(x)\in m(X)$ has also weight $\underline{d}_{1}(x)$. On the other hand, the distance $d_{1}(x,g(x))=d_{1}(x,m_{x})$ also equals $\underline{d}_{1}(x)$ so that one can embed this “abstract” edge as the straight line segment connecting $x$ with $m_{x}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{2}_{1}$.
L259: In case $\underline{d}_{1}(x)=0$ we have $m_{x}=x$ so that the metric quotient $\overline{MC_{1}(X)}$ consists exactly of the set $m(X)$ together with the segments $[x,m_{x}]$ in $\mathbb{R}^{2}_{1}$. We note that the segments $[x,m_{x}]$ and $[y,m_{y}]$ in $\mathbb{R}^{2}_{1}$ cannot cross themselves (unless maybe in the special case $m_{x}=m_{y}$, where they are concatenated) since by Remark cite32†2 L260:  | $$d_{1}(x,y)=d_{1}(x,m_{x})+d_{1}(m_{x},y)=d_{1}(x,m_{x})+d_{1}(m_{x},m_{y})+d_{1}(m_{y},y)$$  |
L261: holds, which means that the points $x,m_{x},m_{y}$ and $y$ lie on a geodesic (shortest path) between $x$ and $y$. (Likewise in the following step $x,m_{x},m^{2}_{x},m^{2}_{y},m_{y}$ and $y$ will lie on a geodesic etc.) Iterating this procedure, which stabilizes after finitely many steps, one obtains an embedding of $\overline{MC(X)}$ into $\mathbb{R}^{2}_{1}$ for the finite subspace $X\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}_{1}$. L273: ## 5 The Tight Span of a Finite Subspace of the Manhattan Plane
L274: In this section, we apply the main theorem of Turaev [[cite16†6 ],Theorem 9.1] to obtain the tight span of a finite subspace $X\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}_{1}$.
